# openhamclock

**Community continuation of HamClock as a browser dashboard — grey line, propagation, spots, satellites**

- **Version recorded:** 26.7.0
- **Categories:** `hf-propagation`
- **Upstream:** <https://github.com/accius/openhamclock>

## What it does

Serves a live station dashboard in your browser: a world map with the grey line, solar and geomagnetic indices, band-condition predictions, DX cluster and POTA spots, satellite passes, and live decodes from WSJT-X on the same machine. It is the community's continuation of HamClock after its author became a Silent Key in January 2026, rewritten as a web application so it runs on anything with a browser — a shack PC, a Pi driving a wall display, or a phone on the same network if you choose to allow that.

## Why you would want it

It is the at-a-glance answer to "which band should I be on right now", and the more active of the two maintained HamClock successors by a wide margin (Q-006). The alternative is `hamclock-next`, an SDL2 rewrite that keeps the original's look and runs as an ordinary desktop program with no Node involved; both are carried, and `propagation` ships this one as the default.

## Before it will work

**Node.js 18 or newer from your distribution** — `hammunition` installs `nodejs` and `npm` from the archive and refuses, naming the version, if what is offered is too old. Every target this project tests qualifies (Ubuntu 24.04 ships 18.19, Debian 13 and Parrot 20.19, Ubuntu 26.04 22.22). **A network connection at install time**: the build fetches about 730 packages from registry.npmjs.org, each checked against the lock file that arrives inside the sha256-verified source archive; nothing else is fetched and no package's install scripts run. After installing, **edit `~/.local/share/hammunition/node/openhamclock/.env`** and set `CALLSIGN` and `LOCATOR` — the first start creates that file from upstream's example with `N0CALL` and `FN31` in it, and the dashboard is centred on the wrong hemisphere until you do. A reinstall or update keeps your `.env`. The engine does not fill those values in yet (station config, D-035, is absolute-path config files only so far); this is a hand step and the profile says so.

## How it installs

- node (needs Node 18+ from the distribution; dependencies fetched from registry.npmjs.org against the lock file) from https://github.com/accius/openhamclock/archive/refs/tags/v26.7.0.tar.gz
  - build dependencies: `nodejs`, `npm`
  - Needs Node.js 18 or newer from the distribution's own `nodejs` package — the engine never fetches Node from NodeSource or nodejs.org, and refuses at plan time when the archive's Node is absent or too old. The build downloads its dependency closure from registry.npmjs.org, verified against the lock file. Built and run 2026-09-01 on Debian 13 (Node 20.19, npm 9.2).

## Known problems

**The server binds to loopback, and `.env` can change that.** The wrapper starts it with `HOST=127.0.0.1`, but openhamclock's own `.env` loader overrides the environment, and the generated `.env` says `HOST=localhost` — same result. Set it to `0.0.0.0` there and the dashboard is reachable from your whole network, which is what you want for a wall display and not what you want on a laptop that also carries security tooling; the choice is yours and it is one line. The same applies to `PORT`: the launcher opens `:3001`, so if you change the port in `.env` the browser tab will point at the old one. **UDP 2237 listens on every interface regardless** — the WSJT-X integration opens it at start and `HOST` does not govern it; set `WSJTX_ENABLED=false` in `.env` if you do not run WSJT-X, or want nothing listening. **Propagation runs in "Standalone mode"**: upstream's build normally downloads an ITU P.533 model as WASM from a moving release tag with a checksum from the same place, which is not a pin, so this build skips it and the server uses its built-in model. A pinned WASM may be carried later as a verified artefact. **The auto-update setting does nothing here**: `AUTO_UPDATE_ENABLED` expects a git clone; leave it `false` and update through `hammunition`, which rebuilds from the next pinned release. The runtime tree is about 140 MB.

## Keeping it current

- probe: github release (`accius/openhamclock`)
- strategy: rebuild
- Upstream releases monthly, on the first Tuesday (its CHANGELOG says so; the changelog itself is frozen and release notes live on GitHub). A rebuild keeps the operator's .env.
